ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: Left arm numbness/tingling with reduced ability to move the left arm (onset ~2 weeks, progressive).
- Symptoms: Numbness and tingling for at least 2 weeks, progressively worse; affects elbow, arm and hand (palmar surface). Numb/tingling in digits 2, 3 and 4 (palmar). Some subjective weakness (difficulty with fine motor tasks, e.g., piano, occasional dropping). Tried massage and warm baths without benefit; took ibuprofen for muscle soreness. Occasional shoulder pain with movement. One transient episode (~20 minutes) of decreased vision in the left eye (partial field loss) about a few weeks ago. Recent fatigue and a viral/flu-like illness ~1 month ago. No seizures, no leg symptoms, walking normal. No acute severe headache, vomiting reported.
- Past medical history: Reports generally healthy. Recent viral/flu-like illness 1 month ago. No chronic neurological diagnoses reported.
- Medications / Allergies: Occasional ibuprofen, vitamin D, occasional melatonin. GP suggested iron supplements which she mostly doesn't take. No allergies mentioned.
- Family / Social history: Father with hypothyroidism and 'autoimmune stuff'; mother with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol. Social: recently started boxing classes (repetitive upper limb use / potential trauma). One episode of heavy alcohol use ~1 month ago. Works, exercises; right-handed.
- Vital signs / exam findings: No formal vital signs or objective exam findings documented in the transcript. Findings derived from history only (subjective weakness, sensory distribution described by patient).
- Labs / imaging: None performed or reported. Doctor recommended urgent neurology referral and brain scan pending.

V: Transient ischemic attack / retinal ischemia (amaurosis fugax) or ischemic stroke: Rationale – patient had a transient ~20-minute unilateral visual field loss (left eye) and currently has focal unilateral arm numbness/weakness, both could reflect transient cerebral or retinal ischemia from an embolic source or carotid pathology.

Carotid artery dissection: Rationale – possible neck/upper-body trauma (boxing), can present with unilateral focal neurological deficits and transient monocular visual loss; though neck pain is not clearly reported.
I: Post-infectious inflammatory neuropathy / brachial neuritis (Parsonage-Turner): Rationale – recent viral illness ~1 month ago followed by focal upper-limb sensory symptoms and weakness; Parsonage-Turner can cause acute/ subacute shoulder/arm pain followed by weakness/sensory loss.

Multiple sclerosis (inflammatory demyelinating disease): Rationale – young/ middle-aged woman with transient visual disturbance (optic neuritis / visual field loss) and focal sensory symptoms that could be separated in time, consistent with demyelinating relapsing disease.
N: Cervical spinal cord or nerve root compression from tumor/metastasis: Rationale – focal unilateral arm sensory and motor symptoms could be caused by a space-occupying lesion affecting nerve roots or cord, though no systemic symptoms or cancer history reported.
Apical lung (Pancoast) tumor with brachial plexus involvement: Rationale – can cause upper-limb neuropathy, but no smoking history or systemic features noted.
D: Cervical radiculopathy from degenerative disc disease / herniated cervical disc: Rationale – repetitive upper-limb use (boxing) raises risk of acute/progressive radicular symptoms; distribution involving arm/elbow/hand digits 2–4 can reflect cervical root compression.
Median neuropathy (carpal tunnel syndrome): Rationale – palmar numbness of digits 2–4 fits median nerve distribution, though carpal tunnel is usually chronic and often nocturnal.
I2: Traumatic/compressive neuropathy from boxing-related injury or overuse (iatrogenic/traumatic): Rationale – new intensive upper-limb activity (boxing) with knuckle injuries and repetitive microtrauma could cause peripheral nerve compression (median, ulnar, radial) or brachial plexus stretch injury.
Toxic neuropathy (alcohol-related): Rationale – heavy alcohol exposure can cause neuropathy but history describes a single binge one month ago, so chronic toxic neuropathy is unlikely.
C: Anatomic predisposition such as thoracic outlet syndrome (congenital variant): Rationale – positional or exertional compression of brachial plexus/vascular structures can cause unilateral arm sensory symptoms, sometimes provoked by exercise (boxing).
A: Multiple sclerosis (autoimmune demyelination): Rationale – MS is autoimmune and can present with separated-in-time neurological deficits including optic involvement and unilateral limb sensory/motor symptoms; family history of autoimmune disease in father noted.

Thyroid-related neuropathy (hypothyroidism-related): Rationale – family history of hypothyroidism; hypothyroid neuropathy tends to be symmetric and chronic, making this less likely but should be considered.
T: Peripheral nerve injury / brachial plexus stretch from boxing trauma: Rationale – repetitive blows, sudden stretches or direct trauma during boxing can produce acute nerve injury causing focal numbness and weakness.
Cervical spine injury (whiplash type) during boxing leading to radiculopathy: Rationale – neck strain/trauma can precipitate radicular symptoms.
E: Vitamin B12 deficiency or other metabolic neuropathy: Rationale – causes neuropathy, usually symmetric and longer-standing; patient takes vitamin D but no B12 reported; iron deficiency (mentioned but not taken) is less likely to cause focal symptoms.

Diabetic neuropathy: Rationale – mother has diabetes (genetic predisposition) but patient does not report diabetes; diabetic neuropathy is typically symmetric and distal rather than focal unilateral symptoms.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Cervical radiculopathy (cervical disc herniation or foraminal compression)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Progressive unilateral arm/forearm/hand numbness and subjective weakness over ~2 weeks after starting boxing fits a mechanical radiculopathy. Sensory distribution (elbow, arm, palmar digits 2–4) and provocation with arm movement/boxing support nerve root irritation. Onset after new repetitive activity increases likelihood.
supporting_evidence: Progressive unilateral sensory symptoms localized to elbow, arm and palmar digits 2–4 over ~2 weeks.
Symptoms provoked/associated with boxing and arm movement; patient reports some shoulder pain with movement.
Functional weakness affecting fine motor tasks (piano) and occasional dropping, consistent with motor involvement.
opposing_evidence: Transient visual loss episode is not explained by isolated cervical radiculopathy.
No focal neck pain or clear precipitating neck injury documented (although absence of recorded neck pain does not exclude radiculopathy).
No objective neurological exam or imaging provided to confirm root compression.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Median neuropathy (carpal tunnel syndrome) or peripheral median nerve compression
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Palmar numbness in digits 2–4 strongly maps to median nerve distribution. Repetitive wrist/hand use in boxing could aggravate a local nerve compression. However the relatively rapid onset (weeks), involvement of elbow/arm, and proximal symptoms are less typical for isolated carpal tunnel.
supporting_evidence: Numbness located on palmar side affecting second, third and fourth fingers — classic median distribution.
Functional impairment (fine motor difficulty, some dropping) consistent with median nerve dysfunction.
opposing_evidence: Symptoms include elbow and proximal arm numbness and subjective weakness, which suggests more proximal lesion (radiculopathy or brachial plexus) rather than isolated carpal tunnel.
Onset over weeks with prior viral illness and transient visual loss better explained by systemic/central causes in differential.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Young-to-middle-aged woman with separated neurological events (transient monocular visual disturbance and subsequent unilateral arm sensory/motor symptoms) consistent with possible demyelinating relapsing disease. Recent viral illness can precede or unmask MS exacerbations. MS remains an important consideration requiring neurologic evaluation and MRI.
supporting_evidence: Transient left-eye visual field loss for ~20 minutes (could reflect optic nerve/visual pathway involvement).
Unilateral sensory symptoms and subjective weakness occurring weeks after the visual event—temporal separation of neuro events is a pattern seen in MS.
Female in the typical age range for MS.
opposing_evidence: MS commonly causes additional central signs (e.g., internuclear ophthalmoplegia, widespread sensory level) and objective neurologic deficits on exam; none documented yet.
Transient monocular visual loss due to ischemia (amaurosis fugax) is an alternative vascular explanation.
No prior history of similar episodes; single transient visual episode was brief (20 minutes) — optic neuritis typically causes more prolonged visual loss and pain with eye movement.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Brachial plexus neuritis (Parsonage-Turner) or traumatic brachial plexus injury
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Post-infectious brachial neuritis can present after a viral illness with shoulder/arm pain followed by weakness and sensory changes. Boxing-related trauma can also cause brachial plexus stretch injury producing similar focal deficits.
supporting_evidence: Recent viral illness ~1 month prior (possible trigger for Parsonage-Turner).
Onset after beginning a new, vigorous activity (boxing) raising risk for traumatic plexus stretch or overuse injury.
Symptoms involve shoulder/arm and include weakness and sensory change.
opposing_evidence: Typical Parsonage-Turner often starts with severe acute shoulder pain followed by weakness; patient did not report an acute severe shoulder pain episode.
Transient monocular visual loss and central symptoms are not explained by isolated brachial plexus pathology.

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Vascular event: TIA / amaurosis fugax or carotid dissection
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: The transient ~20-minute monocular visual field loss is classic for amaurosis fugax (retinal ischemia) from an embolus, often carotid in origin. Focal unilateral arm symptoms could represent a transient ischemic event as well. Carotid dissection is possible with neck trauma from boxing and can present with focal neuro deficits and transient visual symptoms.
supporting_evidence: Transient unilateral visual loss (left eye) lasting ~20 minutes — classic description for amaurosis fugax / TIA.
Unilateral focal arm numbness and weakness occurring in a similar timeframe could represent ischemic events in the same vascular territory.
opposing_evidence: Patient is relatively young and lacks clear vascular risk factors (no diabetes, hypertension reported).
No reported sudden severe neck pain, focal cranial nerve deficits, or persistent focal deficits expected with stroke; no objective findings or imaging yet.
Symptoms have been evolving subacutely for 2 weeks (TIA typically transient and more acute), making purely embolic etiology less straightforward without further workup.
